beats.narration: A cardboard box sits on the bench. Inside: ten freshly manufactured circuit boards, the first ones with the Sprout name printed on them.
Our boards! Our very own boards! Look at the little logo!
Wonderful. Plug one in and let us see Gerald get watered.
No! Nobody plugs anything in. Not yet.
Ada is right to panic. A brand-new board has never been powered. It might have a short circuit, a part soldered backwards, or a design mistake.
Plug it in carelessly, and you can cook the only working prototype.
Today we do bring-up. Slowly, carefully, one piece at a time. It is the most nerve-racking day in any hardware project.
In an ideal project, hardware and software are designed together, reviewed together, and tested together, long before the boards are built.
The software person should review the schematic. Which pins connect to what? Is the button on a pin that can wake the chip from sleep?

beats.narration: Twelve milliamps. Steady. That is about what the datasheet promises when the chip is idle.
That number is music. Now the clock. Then the debugger.
Once the chip is confirmed alive and the debugger can connect, Ada writes the smallest program possible: turn on one LED.
If that works, the processor, the clock, the memory, the programmer, and one output pin all work.
It blinks! It blinks!
From there, each peripheral gets its own small test, one by one. Sensor, button, pump driver. Never everything at once.
The microcontroller's documentation is enormous. There is a datasheet with electrical facts, and a reference manual that describes every peripheral in detail, often more than a thousand pages.
A thousand pages? For a chip the size of my fingernail?
Nobody reads it front to back. You learn to navigate it.
Start at the first page, the summary. Then the pinout. Then the absolute maximum ratings, which tell you what destroys the chip. Respect those numbers like a cliff edge.

beats.narration: The electrical characteristics tables list typical values and worst case limits. Design for the worst case. Typical is what one chip did on a good day in the lab.

beats.narration: The schematic is the circuit diagram of the board. Software engineers who can read one are dramatically more useful in a crisis.
You do not need to design circuits. You need to answer questions. Which pin is the LED on? Does the button pull the pin high or low when pressed?
What voltage does the sensor output?
Symbols help. A zigzag or box is a resistor. Two parallel lines, a capacitor. A triangle with a bar, a diode. Lines that meet with a dot are connected.
Lines that cross without a dot are not.
Schematics are usually split across pages, with labels connecting nets between them. A wire named moisture on page one is the same wire as moisture on page three.
My trick: print the schematic, and highlight every net I touch from software. By the end of bring-up, it is a map of everything the code controls.
I printed it too. I made a poster. It is very decorative.
Reading datasheets and schematics is a skill, and skills need practice.
One of the best places to practice is a cheap hobby board, the kind with a huge community and thousands of tutorials.
That is how I started. A hobby board, a starter kit, and a weekend of making lights blink in the wrong order.
Here is an exercise I give every new engineer. Take a hobby board's schematic, find the chip's datasheet, and trace one pin all the way through.
Hobby libraries hide all of this behind friendly functions, which is great for getting started.

beats.narration: Hardware is fragile in ways software is not. A mistake in code can be undone. A mistake in a circuit can release a little puff of expensive smoke.
Static electricity is the silent killer. You can zap a chip without even feeling the spark. That is why we wear a wrist strap connected to ground.

visual.title: Board safety habits
items: Ground yourself: static kills chips
Power off before changing wires
Check voltages before connecting
Never let probes slip
Keep drinks off the bench

beats.narration: Power off before changing connections. And check the voltage of anything you connect. A five volt signal into a three point three volt pin can damage it.

visual.title: Board safety habits

Never let probes slip
Keep drinks off the bench

beats.narration: The most common accident is a slipping probe: a multimeter tip that skids and shorts two neighboring pins. Clip on wherever you can, instead of holding probes by hand.

beats.narration: When hardware misbehaves, software tools cannot see the problem. You need instruments that measure the physical world.
The multimeter is the first tool you reach for. Is the power rail at the right voltage? Is this wire connected to that pin? Is something shorted?
An oscilloscope draws voltage over time. It shows whether a signal is clean, noisy, too slow, or ringing.
It is how you see the electrical truth behind a digital ones and zeros.
A logic analyzer watches many digital lines at once and decodes them. It can show the bytes passing between the chip and a sensor, with timestamps.
Each tool answers a different question. Learning which one to grab is half of the skill.
There is a cheaper trick too. Spare pins as debug signals. Ada sets a pin high when a function starts and low when it ends.
On the scope, you can see exactly how long the function takes.
That trick costs one line of code and one wire, and it reveals timing that no print statement could ever show, because printing itself takes time.

visual.title: A debug pin on the scope

beats.narration: Instruments can also lie to you. A scope probe adds a tiny load that can change a sensitive circuit. A loose ground clip turns clean signals into noise.

visual.title: A debug pin on the scope

beats.narration: When a measurement looks impossible, check the measurement first.

beats.narration: Once a board works, you need to know it keeps working, and that every board coming off the production line works too.
That means tests that software runs on the hardware itself.
A power-on self test runs at every boot. It must be fast: check memory, check that sensors respond, then get on with the job.

visual.title: Kinds of hardware tests
items: Power-on self test: quick checks at every boot
Manufacturing test: thorough checks per unit
On-demand test: run by a technician

beats.narration: A manufacturing test can be thorough. Each unit gets checked on the factory line before it goes in a box. Here, minutes per unit are affordable; returns are not.

visual.title: Kinds of hardware tests
items: Power-on self test: quick checks at every boot
Manufacturing test: thorough checks per unit
On-demand test: run by a technician

beats.narration: Let me show a classic: testing an external flash memory chip. There are three ways it can fail: the data lines, the address lines, or the memory cells themselves.

visual.title: Kinds of hardware tests
items: Power-on self test: quick checks at every boot
Manufacturing test: thorough checks per unit
On-demand test: run by a technician

beats.narration: First, the data lines. Write a value with exactly one bit set, read it back, and move the bit along.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: If a data line is stuck or shorted, one pattern comes back wrong.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: For address lines, write unique values at addresses that are powers of two, then check none overwrote another. A broken address line makes two addresses secretly the same location.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: And finally, the cells. Fill the memory with a pattern, read it all back. That one is slow, so it is for the factory, not every boot.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: And if a test fails?

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: Then the test must say what failed, clearly. A test that reports, error, is nearly useless.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: A test that reports, data line three stuck low, sends the technician straight to the fault.

visual.title: Walking-ones test on the data bus

beats.narration: To run these tests, the team needs a way to talk to the board. The simplest is a command line over the serial port: type a command, get an answer.
Each command is a row in a table: a name, a function to run, and help text.

visual.title: A tiny command table
lines: typedef struct { const char *name; int (*run)(void); const char *help; } command_t;

beats.narration: The command line reads what you type, finds the matching row, and calls its function.

visual.title: A tiny command table
lines: typedef struct { const char *name; int (*run)(void); const char *help; } command_t;

beats.narration: This is the command pattern: wrapping actions as objects that can be stored, listed, and invoked by name. Adding a command means adding one row, not rewriting the parser.

visual.title: A tiny command table

beats.narration: Type help, and it lists every command. Type pump, and Gerald gets a drink. I love this.

beats.narration: Every function that talks to hardware can fail. Sensors disconnect. Memory wears out. Communication gets garbled. How the code reports errors matters.
The worst thing is inconsistency. One function returns minus one on failure, another returns zero, another returns true. Callers get it wrong, and errors vanish silently.

visual.title: Error handling rules
items: Pick one style and use it everywhere
Return error codes; check them
Fail loudly in development
Recover gracefully in the field
Log what happened

beats.narration: In development, fail loudly, with an assert that stops everything, so bugs are impossible to ignore.
